processing: Made as a Wuyi oolong, partly oxidised, rolled and roasted, as with other rock teas.
harvest_season: Accounts differ: as with other rock teas it is generally a spring picking, while one tea writer describes picking during a warm winter spell.
appearance_dry: Twisted dark strips, as is usual for Wuyi oolong.
appearance_wet: As with other rock teas, open leaves with darkened edges.
taste_profile: Described as light in flavour for a Wuyi oolong; expect a gentle version of the region's mineral, lightly roasted character.

brewing.notes: Its light body rewards slightly less leaf than a heavy rock tea, and short steeps.

vintage_note: Normally sold like other Wuyi oolongs, by harvest year and after the roast has rested. Since picking accounts differ, ask the seller which season the lot comes from.
description:
Bu Zhi Chun means does not know spring. It is a Wuyi oolong with a light reputation, and the name belongs to the group of Wuyi bushes named for when they bud.

The obvious question is what the name implies. Chinese classification places it by budding time without settling the point for the reader, and one tea writer explains it through warm winter spells that fool the bush into sprouting. Treat that explanation as an interpretation.

In the cup, expect less weight than a Rou Gui or a heavy Da Hong Pao. Use a little less leaf, keep steeps short and do not overwhelm it.

It is a small-production name. Ask for harvest year and season, and compare it with a mainstream rock tea to see what the lightness actually means.
history: Bu Zhi Chun is listed among Qing-dynasty Wuyi named bushes in a Chinese history of rock-tea varieties, and modern accounts keep it in the wider family of named bushes. Who selected it and when is not recorded.
